ai.definition: Algorithmic auditing refers to the automated process of verifying artificial intelligence (AI) models for potential biases and adherence to regulatory standards. This technology is designed to ensure that AI systems operate ethically and legally.
ai.howItWorks: Algorithmic auditing employs formal verification methods, which involve rigorous mathematical proofs to check if an AI model meets specified criteria. Additionally, adversarial testing pipelines are used to simulate attacks on the model to identify vulnerabilities or biases. These processes help in ensuring that AI models do not perpetuate unfairness and comply with relevant regulations.
ai.problemSolved: The primary issue addressed by algorithmic auditing is the need for consistent, unbiased, and legally compliant operation of AI systems across various industries such as finance, healthcare, and criminal justice.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves developing and integrating formal verification tools and adversarial testing frameworks into existing AI development workflows. This typically requires specialized software development expertise and access to computational resources.
ai.buildProcess: The build process for algorithmic auditing starts with defining the regulatory requirements and ethical standards that need to be met. Then, formal verification techniques are applied to the AI model's source code or architecture. Adversarial testing is conducted using synthetic data or real-world scenarios to evaluate the robustness of the model against potential biases.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the development of sophisticated formal verification tools, computational resources for adversarial testing, and ongoing maintenance and updates to ensure compliance with evolving regulations.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is positive as regulatory bodies increasingly require transparency and accountability in AI systems. However, widespread adoption faces challenges such as the complexity of formal verification and the need for standardization across different industries.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary by region but generally focus on data privacy, non-discrimination, and ethical use of AI. Compliance with these regulations is a key driver for algorithmic auditing.
ai.risks: Risks include the potential for false positives or negatives in formal verification, difficulty in creating comprehensive adversarial testing scenarios, and the complexity of integrating these systems into existing development pipelines.
ai.profitability: Profitability depends on the specific application and market. While regulatory compliance can be a significant driver, the cost of implementation may limit widespread adoption initially.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments could include more efficient formal verification techniques, increased automation in adversarial testing, and integration with AI development platforms to streamline the auditing process.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and computational resources required for formal verification and adversarial testing.

glossary.def: A method used in algorithmic auditing that involves the use of mathematical proofs to ensure AI models meet specific criteria.
A process where AI models are tested against simulated attacks to identify potential biases or vulnerabilities.

subsystems.name: Access and data layer
subsystems.role: connects securely to the AI system under audit and gathers the inputs, outputs and metadata needed for testing.

subsystems.name: Test and metric engine
subsystems.role: runs quantitative checks for fairness, robustness and accuracy.

subsystems.name: Adversarial and counterfactual testing
subsystems.role: probes how the model behaves under manipulated or alternative inputs to expose hidden failures.

subsystems.name: Formal verification module
subsystems.role: mathematically proves that a model satisfies certain properties, where feasible.

subsystems.name: Compliance mapping and reporting
subsystems.role: translates technical findings into regulatory language and evidence.

subsystems.name: Continuous monitoring
subsystems.role: tracks a deployed model for drift, emerging bias and performance decay.

buildSteps.title: Define audit scope and regulatory context
buildSteps.detail: Identify which laws apply (for example the EU AI Act or GDPR), what decisions the model affects, and which groups could be harmed.

buildSteps.title: Secure access to model and data
buildSteps.detail: Obtain API keys, model weights and training or representative data under confidentiality agreements.

buildSteps.title: Instrument the model
buildSteps.detail: Set up logging, input/output capture, and hooks for internal activations if the model is open to inspection.

buildSteps.title: Develop test suites
buildSteps.detail: Implement fairness metrics, robustness checks against input noise, and accuracy benchmarks for relevant subgroups.

buildSteps.title: Run adversarial and counterfactual tests
buildSteps.detail: Generate worst-case inputs and alternative scenarios to surface hidden failures or discriminatory patterns.

buildSteps.title: Apply formal verification where possible
buildSteps.detail: For critical properties, use solvers to prove bounds or the absence of certain behaviours, acknowledging limits on large models.

buildSteps.title: Analyse and interpret results
buildSteps.detail: Statistically validate findings, assess severity, and trace issues to data, training or deployment causes.

buildSteps.title: Map findings to regulations
buildSteps.detail: Align each issue with specific legal requirements and assemble the evidence needed for a compliance case.

buildSteps.title: Generate audit report and remediation plan
buildSteps.detail: Document findings, recommend fixes, and set up ongoing monitoring to confirm they work.

prerequisites.tech: Access to model internals or APIs
prerequisites.why: closed models can be probed through APIs, but full access to weights and training data gives deeper audits.

pathway.milestone: ad-hoc audits and open-source fairness toolkits
pathway.unlocks: practical detection of bias and robustness problems in individual models.

pathway.milestone: standardised audit protocols and certification schemes
pathway.unlocks: comparable, repeatable audits that regulators and buyers can trust.

pathway.unlocks: widespread adoption of auditing as a legal requirement rather than a voluntary check.
